archetype: Mono-black sacrifice attrition engine with a drain clock and a tutor-dependent finish — Yawgmoth, Thran Physician as a mana-free repeatable draw engine that converts renewable bodies into cards, Nest of Scarabs replacing the bodies it spends, an each-opponent drain converting deaths into a table-wide clock, and two kills (Blowfly + Nest, and the Mikaeus undying package) that the five-tutor suite reaches in roughly a third of games rather than by drawing into them

role_assignment.default_role: CONTROL — the inevitability seat, and the deck should stop apologising for it. strategy:whos-the-beatdown's operational test is 'who has inevitability? — whoever loses the long game must be the beatdown', and this deck does not lose the long game to a fair table: Yawgmoth's ability costs no mana ('Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw a card'), so every spare body is a card at instant speed, forever. strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock names exactly this shape — 'four-player games trend long, so inevitability compounds — engines are the default winning plan' — and strategy:card-advantage's Commander correction says 'engines that out-draw three players are the format's defining advantage'. Read the goldfish sheet at its own horizon: max_turn is 10, and strategy:deckbuilding.curve puts the format there too ('Commander games average 7–10 turns'). By turn 10 the enabler classes arrive at 78.6% renewable fodder unassisted / 92.3% tutor-assisted, 78.0% / 92.1% a free sac outlet, 73.5% / 90.6% an ignition source, 60.8% / 85.4% a drain, and 53.0% / 82.0% engine mana; the commander is on the battlefield in 98.6% of games (142 of 10,000 never cast him), mean turn 4.287, and 72.1% of games cast him exactly on turn four. That is a control deck's opening in every column. Role is seat-relative: you are the control against fair midrange and the beatdown against anything that wins before turn seven.
role_assignment.pivot_trigger: BODIES, counted before the first activation. Every one of the four engine stacks that ran to exhaustion ended the same way — stack 005's final state says the run ended 'by body exhaustion (no creature other than Yawgmoth left to sacrifice - not life, not library)' — so the go decision is body arithmetic, which is precisely the form strategy:critical-mass.storm-math prescribes: 'the go decision is arithmetic done *before* the first spell: the chain you can bank on versus the storm count, bodies, or damage the payoff needs for lethal. Count only hand and board; expected draws are a bonus, not a plan.' The exchange rate is verified and unflattering: with Yawgmoth + Nest of Scarabs + an each-opponent drain, the board's number is SEVEN drains, i.e. seven life from each opponent (stacks 002 and 003, both checker-pass; 28 total from a four-opponent pod of 160). One assembly takes a table from 40 to 33. So the pivot is NOT 'can I kill the pod' — it is 'can I kill ONE seat', and the correct trigger is: the lowest life total at the table is at or under (spare bodies you can sacrifice) + (counters your surviving toughness can absorb). strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window sets the bar for going at all — 'Prefer win attempts that leave a rebuilt position if they fail' — and this engine always does, because the fallback is a fistful of cards. Two accelerants change the count: a counter-sink whose toughness exceeds 1 (South Wind Avatar's 4 toughness is worth exactly +4 activations, verified stack 005) and Yawgmoth's own '{B}{B}, Discard a card: Proliferate', worth exactly one extra drain, 8/32 instead of 7/28 (stack 002's proliferate variant, stated separately from the board invariant). The SECOND pivot is the tutor, and it is a separate decision with its own timing — see the tutor engine.

engines.engine: THE ENGINE, and it is a draw engine before it is a kill. 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw a card' costs NO MANA — the price is life and bodies. Four checker-passed stacks record the draw explicitly: stack 005 runs 8 completed activations and ends with cards_drawn 8, library 52, you at 39 life (40 start, -1 per activation x8, +1 per lifegain event x7). That is a Necropotence-rate draw engine attached to a 2/4 body, repeatable at instant speed, on any turn, under any tax. strategy:card-advantage calls card advantage 'very likely, the single most important concept in competitive Magic' (Duke) and its Commander correction names 'engines that out-draw three players' as the format's defining advantage. Protection from Humans is load-bearing in both directions: it makes Yawgmoth untargetable by his own ability, which is what bounds every engine stack — 'Yawgmoth is 2/4 but his protection from Humans makes him untargetable by his own ability (702.16b, 113.7)' (stack 003) — and it blanks a slice of the format's creature removal.
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json); verified stacks 002/003/004/005 (all checker.verdict == pass), which record activation counts, draws and life ledgers; goldfish commander mean_cast_turn 4.287, median 4, cast_turn_histogram 7208 of 10,000 on turn four and 142 never cast by max_turn 10

engines.piece: Nest of Scarabs + Yawgmoth, Thran Physician
engines.engine: The body-neutral half of the loop, and the deck's real hub. 'Whenever you put one or more -1/-1 counters on a creature, create that many 1/1 black Insect creature tokens' returns one body for the counter each activation spends — but only one, and only after the death: stack 004 states the arithmetic flatly, 'killing one of your own creatures makes the activation minus one body by plain arithmetic — two of your creatures leave, Nest returns one'. The loop is therefore body-NEUTRAL only while the counter lands on something that survives it (an opponent's creature, or your own toughness-2-or-greater body), and body-NEGATIVE otherwise. Stack 006 (pass) adds the ruling that widens the engine: a creature that ENTERS with a -1/-1 counter DOES trigger the Nest, via CR 122.6/122.6a — 'a reference to counters being put on an object covers an object that is GIVEN counters as it enters the battlefield' — which is why Persist ('Return target nonlegendary creature card from your graveyard to the battlefield with a -1/-1 counter on it') is a Nest trigger as well as a reanimation. The same stack names the trap: Fume Spitter is a 1/1, enters as a 0/0 and is dead to state-based actions before the trigger resolves, so you keep the Insect and not the body. Structural precision worth carrying into print: Skullclamp's '+1/-1' is a static modification, NOT a counter, so equipping does not trigger the Nest.
engines.evidence: oracle text; verified stacks 002/003/004/005 (bound and body arithmetic) and 006 (CR 122.6 entering-counters ruling); deck-facts notes Nest of Scarabs has NO entry in synergy_graph.json at all — the retrieval graph is blind to this deck's hub

engines.piece: Bastion of Remembrance / Zulaport Cutthroat / Mirkwood Bats / South Wind Avatar (each-opponent drains) versus Blood Artist (single-target)
engines.engine: The payoff layer, and the gap between its two halves is measured, not argued. strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry names 'wide alpha strikes, loops, commander-damage kills, and each-opponent drains' as 'the payoffs that actually scale', and strategy:life-as-resource.philosophy-of-fire's Commander correction is the same finding from the other side: 'raw cards-to-damage math collapses against ~120 combined life — reach must scale (each-opponent drains, commander damage, damage doublers) or be held as targeted finishing rather than the plan'. The deck's own stacks price it: the same board yields 28 opposing life through Bastion (stack 002) or Zulaport (stack 003) and EIGHT through Blood Artist (stack 004) — a 3.5x penalty for 'target player loses 1 life' against 'each opponent loses 1 life'. Stack 004's verdict is 'NOT A KILL, AND NOT EVEN CLOSE'. Two further verified constraints: Zulaport caps at 7 because it is itself a body that must eventually be sacrificed and its own death banks the last drain via CR 603.6c/603.10a; and South Wind Avatar routes through lifegain, so per CR 119.9 an Insect killed by its own -1/-1 counter dies at toughness 0, gains 0 life, and produces NO drain — seven nonzero gains from eight death triggers (stack 005). Mirkwood Bats belongs in this list but meters something different from the other three and its rate is loop-specific, not a blanket multiplier — see the candidate lines. Blood Artist earns its slot as removal-adjacent reach and a Snuff Out / Fatal Push / Dismember / Deadly Rollick partner (43 intra-deck synergy edges, most of them 'Removal + Death Trigger'), not as the payoff you assemble toward. The class as a whole is in hand by turn 10 in 60.8% of games unassisted, 85.4% with a tutor.
engines.evidence: oracle text; verified stacks 002 (28), 003 (28), 004 (8, refuted as a kill), 005 (28 with the CR 119.9 zero-toughness carve-out); deck-facts synergy block (43 intra-deck edges); goldfish 'A drain drawn — the payoff every loop routes through' 0.608 / 0.854 assisted by turn 10

engines.piece: Toughness that survives a counter — South Wind Avatar (3/4), Retched Wretch (4/2), Grave Titan, Carnifex Demon, Massacre Girl, and any opponent's creature
engines.engine: The scarcest resource in the deck, and the one that converts a value engine into a burst turn. Because the loop is body-neutral only while the counter lands on something that lives, every point of toughness above 1 is an extra activation, an extra card and an extra drain. Stack 005 measures it exactly: 'The Avatar's 4 toughness extends the bound by exactly +4 activations (4 of 8) and supplies all of the damage.' Stack 002 records the same effect from the other side of the table — an opponent's 2/2 'does not bound the engine, it EXTENDS it by two activations'. Retched Wretch is the deck's purest expression of this: a 4/2 that soaks a counter and lives at 3/1, then, when it dies with that counter still on it, returns — so it pays two bodies and two Nest triggers from one slot. strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math's advice reads as a design brief for this package: 'buy resilience instead of restraint where you can — high toughness, indestructible and regeneration, token rebuilders, threats that replace themselves.' Practical consequence for the pilot: an opponent's untapped board is FUEL, and a table with no creatures is the worst board state this engine can face.
engines.evidence: verified stack 005 (+4 activations, ceiling proved by case exhaustion); verified stack 002 (opponent's 2/2 extends by two); oracle text and printed P/T for Retched Wretch (4/2) and South Wind Avatar (3/4) in cards.json

engines.piece: Ophiomancer + Bitterblossom + Sedgemoor Witch + Grave Titan + Carrier Thrall + Bloodghast + Butcher Ghoul + Geralf's Messenger (the fodder economy)
engines.engine: The enabler class the whole plan rests on, and goldfish labels it the measured bottleneck: RENEWABLE FODDER drawn is 78.6% by turn 10 unassisted and 92.3% with a tutor, mean turn 2.671 — the earliest and highest of every target on the sheet in both columns. strategy:mulligans.engine-hands is the governing frame: 'Payoffs without the enabler are blanks until the engine exists; enablers without payoffs at least dig toward them — an asymmetry that usually favors keeping the enabler-heavy hand', and its Commander correction, '100-card singleton means you mulligan to enabler *classes*, not named cards'. Ophiomancer is the standout and is under-rated by every count in the artifacts: 'At the beginning of EACH upkeep, if you control no Snakes, create a 1/1 black Snake creature token with deathtouch' — in a four-player pod that is up to four free deathtouch bodies per turn cycle if each one is spent before the next upkeep. Carrier Thrall is fodder that pays twice, dying into 'a 1/1 colorless Eldrazi Scion... Sacrifice this token: Add {C}' — a body and a mana. The board fills accordingly: goldfish mean bodies is 3.984 by turn 6 and 6.625 by turn 10. deck-facts counts 28 threat:body and 10 threat:tokens against 11 sac-cost and 9 sac-outlet: the enabler side of strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density's 7-8 enablers / 10-12 enhancers is comfortably over-supplied, which is correct for a deck whose engine eats its own board.
engines.evidence: oracle text; goldfish targets 'RENEWABLE FODDER drawn (the measured bottleneck)' 0.786 / 0.923 assisted, 'A free repeatable sacrifice outlet drawn (not counting Yawgmoth)' 0.780 / 0.921, 'An ignition source drawn' 0.735 / 0.906, all by turn 10; mean_bodies_by_turn; deck-facts role histogram

engines.piece: Phyrexian Altar + Ashnod's Altar + Pitiless Plunderer + Phyrexian Tower + Carrier Thrall's Scion (engine mana)
engines.engine: The class that converts a death into castable mana, and the deck's weakest link by its own numbers in both columns: ENGINE MANA drawn is 53.0% by turn 10 unassisted and 82.0% tutor-assisted — the lowest of every enabler class on the sheet, 25 points behind fodder unassisted and still 10 behind it with a tutor. That matters because Yawgmoth himself needs none of it, but everything ELSE does: redeploying after a sweeper, casting the drain you just drew, paying '{B}{B}, Discard a card: Proliferate' for the eighth drain, and paying for the tutor itself on the turn you want it. It is also where the deck's remaining unverified infinites live — Ashnod's Altar and Phyrexian Altar are both halves of Mikaeus two-card lines. Mana development is otherwise healthy: goldfish mean available mana 3.927 on turn 4, 5.241 on turn 6 and 7.109 on turn 10 against a curve with nothing at mana value 5 and only three cards above four, and mana_analysis puts on-curve black at 0.895 from lands alone, 0.970 counting rocks and dorks.
engines.evidence: goldfish target 'ENGINE MANA drawn — turns a creature death into castable black' 0.530 / 0.820 assisted by turn 10; mean_available_mana_by_turn; mana_analysis on_curve_probability {lands_only B 0.895, with_rocks_and_dorks B 0.970}; deck-facts curve {1:15, 2:16, 3:20, 4:10, 6:3}

engines.piece: Demonic Tutor + Vampiric Tutor + Beseech the Mirror + Diabolic Intent + Insatiable Avarice
engines.engine: THE FINISH. Not a consistency tax on a deck that wins some other way — the tutors ARE how this deck converts, and the sheet now measures it. strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors quotes Commander Mechanic — a tutor is 'essentially an additional copy of any card in our deck' — and formalises it: 'k tutors plus the card act like k+1 copies of *every* card.' Nest of Scarabs is a singleton hub with no redundancy whatsoever in the 99; five unrestricted tutors make it behave like six copies, and the goldfish model now simulates that directly, treating a drawn and affordable tutor as a wildcard that 'fills ONE missing any_of group. Consumed once, mana paid, and a tutor that puts the card on top of the library costs a turn.' By turn 10 that moves EITHER kill assembled from 4.6% to 31.4%, Blowfly + Nest from 2.7% to 32.1%, and the Mikaeus line from 1.8% to 24.8%. The 27-point gap on the headline number is not an artifact of the model — it is the measured value of the tutor package, and it is the largest single contribution any five slots make to this deck. Two disciplines follow. The section's honest cost is live: 'tutoring is fewer slots but costs board impact and a turn of tempo' — Lowry, 'the more tutors you play, the less actual cards you get to play' — so the tutor is not a turn-three play, it is the card you spend once the engine is stable and you know which half is missing. And a tutor cannot fetch itself: the 'A tutor drawn' row is identical in both columns at 61.7% by turn 10, which is the real ceiling on the whole effect and the reason Diabolic Intent's sacrifice cost (free in this shell, a real card anywhere else) earns its slot.
engines.evidence: bracket_report tutors [Beseech the Mirror, Demonic Tutor, Diabolic Intent, Insatiable Avarice, Vampiric Tutor]; goldfish meta.model_assumptions (tutor-wildcard clause, quoted verbatim) and the paired unassisted/assisted target figures by turn 10

engines.piece: Victimize + Persist + Animate Dead + Agadeem's Awakening + Phyrexian Reclamation + Bloodghast + Butcher Ghoul (the rebuild package)
engines.engine: Five recursion slots plus self-returning bodies, which is what lets this deck treat a sweeper as a payment rather than a loss. strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math's Commander correction is the instruction: 'assume the wrath — over a four-player game one is near-certain — so deploy in waves, hold a rebuild package, and when possible let another player's board be the reason it gets cast.' With an each-opponent drain on the battlefield a wrath is a drain trigger per body — the deck is one of the few whose board WANTS to die — so the sweeper that actually costs you is the one aimed at Yawgmoth or the enchantment removal aimed at Nest of Scarabs, neither of which recursion answers. Persist is the highest-value line in the package on this list because verified stack 006 makes it a Nest trigger as well as a reanimation, and because a 4/2 Retched Wretch or a 3/4 South Wind Avatar returned with a -1/-1 counter SURVIVES the counter, where the same spell on Fume Spitter buys only the Insect.
engines.evidence: deck-facts role histogram (recursion 5, protection:self 3); verified stack 006 (entering counters trigger the Nest); oracle text and printed P/T

engines.piece: Lightning Greaves + Malakir Rebirth + Supernatural Stamina + Deadly Rollick
engines.engine: Commander insurance, priced against a hub the whole plan routes through. strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance sets the test — 'how critical is the commander to the plan, and what removal this table actually runs' — and gives the answer shape for this deck directly: 'the engine's hub justifies constant protection down plus a held response on the pivot turn — assume every held answer appears the moment you commit'. Lightning Greaves is the constant layer (and its haste matters: Yawgmoth's ability needs no tap, but the Greaves cost is zero to re-arm); Malakir Rebirth and Supernatural Stamina are the held responses, both of which return the creature to the battlefield and therefore both of which reset a commander rather than paying the tax. The recast tax is the price of getting it wrong: each return trip adds {2} per prior command-zone cast on top of a four-mana body, and goldfish mean available mana is 3.927 on turn 4 — a single recast costs a whole turn of development. One caution the artifacts support: Lightning Greaves grants shroud, so while it is equipped you cannot target Yawgmoth with your own Malakir Rebirth or Supernatural Stamina.
engines.evidence: oracle text (Lightning Greaves, Malakir Rebirth // Malakir Mire, Supernatural Stamina, Deadly Rollick); deck-facts role histogram protection:self 3; goldfish mean_available_mana_by_turn

candidate_missing_lines.title: Blowfly Infestation + Nest of Scarabs + Mirkwood Bats: does a creation-triggered drain monetise the loop that a death-triggered drain cannot?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: The highest-value open question on this deck. Verified stack 001 proved the Blowfly + Nest loop is genuinely unbounded but DRAINLESS on its board, for a precise reason: state-based actions kill the counter-bearing Insect before the Nest trigger resolves, so at the instant Blowfly's mandatory 'put a -1/-1 counter on target creature' needs a target the only creature left is the drainer, which therefore dies on iteration one — 'Total drain: exactly 3 per opponent'. Every death-triggered drain in the 99 fails that way. Mirkwood Bats does not meter deaths: 'Whenever you create or sacrifice a token, each opponent loses 1 life' pays on CREATION, so every Nest token the loop makes would drain each opponent whether or not the token survives to die. Note precisely what this does NOT claim: Blowfly's loop kills its tokens through state-based actions from -1/-1 counters and SACRIFICES nothing, so Bats collects the creation half only — one trigger per iteration here, not the two it would collect on a Yawgmoth activation. Bats is also a 2/3, so it absorbs two of Blowfly's forced counters instead of one. Two sub-questions the scenario must settle rather than assume: whether Nest creating N tokens in one event triggers Bats once or N times, and the exact iteration count and exit ordering with Bats plus stack 001's prescribed two spare bodies. deck-facts reports no contained combo line involving Mirkwood Bats — combo_details lists it only with cards outside this 99 — so nothing in the data grants this.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Mirkwood Bats + Yawgmoth + Nest of Scarabs: two triggers per activation on THIS line specifically
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: The structural asymmetry made concrete, and it is line-specific — it does not generalise to every loop in the deck. Yawgmoth's cost is 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature', which IS a sacrifice, so paying it with an Insect gives Bats its sacrifice half; the Nest token that follows gives it the creation half. On a plain reading Bats therefore sees BOTH halves of one Yawgmoth activation where Bastion of Remembrance and Zulaport Cutthroat see only the death. If that holds, the same board that stacks 002 and 003 measured at seven drains / 28 opposing life would produce materially more with Bats, and Bats would be the correct drain to tutor for rather than Bastion. The reading is not free: Bats does not trigger at all when a token dies to its own -1/-1 counter (that is neither a creation nor a sacrifice), which is a different carve-out from the CR 119.9 zero-toughness carve-out stack 005 found for South Wind Avatar, and the two must not be blended. The scenario should reuse the 002/003 board verbatim so the numbers are comparable, and should state explicitly that the rate found here is not the rate on the Blowfly loop.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Mikaeus, the Unhallowed + a free sacrifice outlet + a -1/-1 counter source: are the eight two-card infinites that set this deck's bracket floor actually real?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: bracket_report.json forces floor 4 on two independent drivers, one of which is '8 two-card infinite(s); 8 assemble at mana value <= 6'. All eight are Mikaeus pairs, all are tagged bracket 1 by the source data, and NONE is verified. The mechanism they presumably rely on is the annihilation of a +1/+1 counter by a -1/-1 counter, which would re-enable undying — a mechanism this deck supplies in eight different ways (Yawgmoth's own counter, Blowfly Infestation, Sinister Gnarlbark's blight, Necropede, Fume Spitter, Skinrender, Soul Snuffers, Carnifex Demon) but which the two-card listing does not name. Three Commander Spellbook claims about this exact deck have already been overturned by the checker: 'Near-infinite' on Yawgmoth + Nest + Blood Artist (stack 004: eight life, refuted), on Yawgmoth + Nest + South Wind Avatar (stack 005: 'Spellbook's Near-infinite tag is wrong for this board'), and the Blowfly + Nest kill (stack 001: unbounded but drainless). The practical weight of this line is no longer negligible — goldfish rates it at 1.8% unassisted and 24.8% tutor-assisted by turn 10 — which raises the stakes rather than lowering them: a quarter of games now route through a line nothing has verified, and it is also half of what names this deck Optimized.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Ophiomancer in a four-player pod: four free deathtouch bodies per turn cycle, and what South Wind Avatar costs it
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: 'At the beginning of each upkeep, if you control no Snakes, create a 1/1 black Snake creature token with deathtouch' — each upkeep, not each of your upkeeps. If the intervening-if is satisfied on both the look-back check and resolution each time a free sac outlet has already eaten the previous Snake, Ophiomancer is the deck's largest renewable fodder source by a wide margin, worth up to four bodies and four drain triggers per round for zero mana. It also holds the deck's one live internal conflict: South Wind Avatar is a Snake Spirit Avatar, so while it is on the battlefield Ophiomancer makes nothing at all. The scenario should establish the per-round body count with a free outlet, and settle whether sacrificing the Avatar mid-engine (which stack 005 already shows happens — it dies to its fourth counter) restores Ophiomancer's trigger on the very next upkeep. The tension is real and is not resolved by anything currently in the 99.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Skullclamp on a 1/1 Insect: a repeatable draw-two that costs {1} and one Nest token
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: 'Equipped creature gets +1/-1' kills a 1/1 token on equip and 'Whenever equipped creature dies, draw two cards' pays for it — a {1} draw-two plus a death trigger, repeatable for every token Nest of Scarabs makes and every Faerie, Snake or Pest the fodder engine produces. It is a second, mana-priced draw engine running alongside Yawgmoth's free one, and it is the deck's answer to a turn where Yawgmoth is not on the battlefield. Two points the scenario must nail because prose will get them wrong otherwise: Skullclamp's +1/-1 is a static modification and NOT a -1/-1 counter, so equipping does not trigger the Nest and does not enable Blowfly Infestation's intervening-if; and the token dying while equipped is a death, so it does feed Bastion, Zulaport and South Wind Avatar (a token at toughness 0 from Skullclamp raises the same CR 119.9 lifegain question stack 005 answered for counters). deck-facts contains no combo line pairing Skullclamp with anything in this 99.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Retched Wretch under Yawgmoth: how many bodies and how many Insects does one slot actually pay?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: A 4/2 whose dies-trigger reads 'if it had a -1/-1 counter on it, return it to the battlefield under its owner's control and it loses all abilities'. On a plain reading it soaks one counter and lives at 3/1 (one Nest token), then dies to the second or to a sacrifice while carrying that counter and returns as a vanilla 4/2 (a second body, and a second counter-sink) — but the returned object has lost the trigger, so the cycle does not repeat. Verified stack 006 already establishes that Persist returning it with a counter triggers the Nest; unlike Fume Spitter it survives that counter. The scenario should state the exact body-and-token yield per copy and whether the returned object can be a Blowfly Infestation target twice, because this is the template for what a good counter-sink looks like in this archetype and the number will be quoted.

matchup_frames.vs_sweeper_control: The best matchup on the sheet, and the one place the deck should be actively happy. strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math's Commander correction is 'assume the wrath — over a four-player game one is near-certain — so deploy in waves, hold a rebuild package, and when possible let another player's board be the reason it gets cast', and its central advice, 'buy resilience instead of restraint where you can — high toughness, indestructible and regeneration, token rebuilders, threats that replace themselves', describes this 99 almost line by line: five recursion slots, self-returning bodies (Bloodghast's landfall, Butcher Ghoul's undying, Retched Wretch), and per-upkeep token rebuilders. With an each-opponent drain on the battlefield a sweeper is a drain per body — the deck is one of very few whose board profits from dying, and goldfish has 6.625 bodies on the table by turn 10. The two cards that actually cost you are removal aimed at Yawgmoth (pay the recast tax, or pre-empt it per strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance) and enchantment removal aimed at Nest of Scarabs, which no recursion in the list answers — and which is the one board state where the tutor is a rebuild rather than a finish. Deploy the fodder freely and the hub late.
matchup_frames.vs_stax: Structurally better than it looks on one axis and structurally awful on another, and the pilot must know which. Yawgmoth's ability costs NO MANA, so Sphere effects, Winter Orb and Rule of Law do not touch the engine once it is online — strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial's warning that 'decks built on many cheap spells per turn are hit hardest: taxes attack the velocity math directly' applies to getting the hub down, and to casting the tutor, not to running the engine. What genuinely beats this deck is the class it cannot answer: 'Breadth before depth: three opponents mean every permanent type appears, so cover the classes — creature, artifact, enchantment, graveyard, land — before doubling any' (strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite), and mono-black covers exactly one of those classes. The 99 has no artifact removal, no enchantment removal, no counterspell, and one graveyard answer (Bojuka Bog). A Cursed Totem, Pithing Needle or Rest in Peace is a hard stop with no out in the maindeck. strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial then forces the role — 'you rarely own the long game under an assembling lock, so you are the beatdown, racing the lock's completion' — so against a stax start, abandon the grind, spend the tutor early rather than optimally, and go for a seat before the second and third pieces land.
matchup_frames.vs_aggro: Favoured, and the reason is arithmetic rather than answers. strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry: 'aggro's math is worst hit — ~120 combined life behind three defenses makes incremental combat damage a losing plan'. Against you specifically it is worse: your board is renewable fodder, chump blocking is free because a death is a card (Yawgmoth) and a drain, and the deck fields deathtouch on Ophiomancer's Snake, South Wind Avatar and Grave Titan. deck-facts counts 10 removal:debuff, 3 removal:spot, 3 removal:sweeper — the -1/-1 package doubles as removal, which is what lets a deck with only seven or eight dedicated interaction spells survive early pressure. Two disciplines: strategy:life-as-resource says early life points are cheap and late ones priceless, and this engine pays 1 life per activation on top of Necropotence, Black Market Connections and four pain lands, so track how much of your total the engine has already spent before you take a race seriously; and let the aggro player's creatures live where you can, because an opponent's board EXTENDS your engine by absorbing counters (verified stack 002).
matchup_frames.vs_combo: The worst matchup, and the frame should say so. The interaction suite is four free-or-cheap answers (Deadly Rollick, Snuff Out, Fatal Push, Dismember) and every one of them targets a creature — against a noncreature kill the deck has literally nothing, and there are no counterspells. strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy's countervailing rule therefore binds hard here: 'held answers rot — against combo, or lethal already on board, the last profitable moment is now.' Do not hold Snuff Out for a better target. The compensating plan is speed and cover, and it is now a real plan rather than a hope: the commander is on the battlefield in 98.6% of games at a mean of turn 4.287, a drain is in hand by turn 10 in 85.4% with a tutor, and a kill assembles in 31.4% — so racing a combo deck is a coin the deck can actually flip if it stops waiting for the perfect board. strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection is the other half — 'combo decks look non-threatening while advancing in secret, which is exactly why experienced tables hit the quiet ramp player' — read as a warning about yourself: a Yawgmoth on the battlefield reads as a combo tell to any experienced table, so spend the deflection budget on the actual combo player and take your window while three players' interaction is pointed elsewhere.
matchup_frames.vs_stax_note_on_horizon: Cross-matchup discipline on the numbers: max_turn in the sim is 10 and strategy:deckbuilding.curve puts the format at 'Commander games average 7–10 turns', so every rate in these frames is quoted at turn 10 unless an early-game claim genuinely needs turn 6. Quoting a turn-6 figure as the deck's rate understates every enabler class by 10 to 17 points and the kill by half.

distribution_notes: 36 land copies across 15 entries (22 of them Swamp), 64 nonland, 100 copies from 79 entries — deck-facts counts copies, and the land figure must always be quoted as 36, never as the 15 entries. Curve {1:15, 2:16, 3:20, 4:10, 6:3}: nothing at all at mana value 5, only three cards above four (Grave Titan, Mikaeus, Carnifex Demon), and 51 of 64 spells at three or less. Against strategy:deckbuilding.curve's measured Commander shape — MtGDS' EDHREC pull at 15.7 two-drops and 15.4 three-drops in the average deck, and more cards at the commander's own mana value than the global curve (9.7 four-drops for four-mana commanders) — this list is dead on at two (16) and at four (10) and heavy at three (20), which is where the ignition, the drains and the Nest all sit. The same section supplies the horizon this frame reads every rate at: 'Commander games average 7–10 turns', which is why the sim's max_turn of 10 is the yardstick and turn 6 is a checkpoint, not a verdict. Its rule 'Build to hit 2, 4 and 6 mana reliably' is satisfied at the low end and largely moot at the high: goldfish mean available mana is 3.927 on turn 4, 5.241 on turn 6 and 7.109 on turn 10, and the deck has almost nothing to spend six on beyond a second tutor and a proliferate. Colour is trivial and should not be discussed as if it were a problem: one colour, 70 black pips across 53 cards, max 3 pips, source target 36 against 35 black land sources (45 counting nonland producers), on-curve black 0.895 from lands alone and 0.970 with rocks and dorks, four lands entering tapped, no restricted mana anywhere. Roles: 28 threat:body and 10 threat:tokens supply the fodder; 11 sac-cost and 9 sac-outlet supply the conversion; 6 wincon:drain and 5 payoff:counters supply the payoff; 5 recursion and 5 tutor:unrestricted supply the resilience and, on the sim's own accounting, most of the conversion. The interaction count needs reading with care — deck-facts reports 10 removal:debuff, but most of that decad (Fume Spitter, Skinrender, Soul Snuffers, Necropede, Sinister Gnarlbark, Carnifex Demon) is ENGINE IGNITION that happens to shrink an opposing creature, so the deck's dedicated interaction is nearer seven or eight, the very bottom of the 'at least 8-10 removal spells' baseline in strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite and covering one permanent class out of five. Role coverage is 98.73% with one card the taxonomy has no pattern for (Supernatural Stamina) — absence of a role is not absence of function. Two artifact cautions for anyone writing from the graphs: synergy_graph.json contributes 43 edges inside this deck and is a global top-10 shortlist rather than a fit score, and it has NO entry at all for Nest of Scarabs, Demonic Tutor, Insatiable Avarice, Toxic Deluge or Vampiric Tutor — the deck's central engine card is invisible to it.
overall_assessment: It is an attrition engine whose finish is tutor-dependent rather than rare, and the two numbers have to be printed together: the deck assembles one of its two kills by turn 10 in 4.6% of games on its draws alone and in 31.4% once the tutors are allowed to fetch the missing half — and that 27-point gap IS the measured value of the five tutor slots. strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors is not decoration on that figure, it is the mechanism: a tutor is 'essentially an additional copy of any card in our deck', so 'k tutors plus the card act like k+1 copies of *every* card', and a singleton Nest of Scarabs behaving like six copies is exactly what turns 2.7% into 32.1% on the Blowfly line and 1.8% into 24.8% on the Mikaeus one. A finish that lands roughly a third of the time is a finish. strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density's opening — 'Value is not a win' — is the standard this deck now passes rather than the criticism it once invited, and the same section's cEDH rule describes the shape it passes with: Eisenherz's 'two primary combos, a Plan A and Plan B, never more than two *unconnected* ones', reconciled by layering, 'overlap pieces, so five cards support four combos'. There are exactly two kills here and they share almost their whole support structure — free sacrifice outlets, -1/-1 sources, the same tutors. What survives from the attrition reading is the ordering, and it is the part the pilot most needs. strategy:critical-mass.storm-math still governs: 'Separate ceiling from median: the full storm kill is the ceiling; the median game is the value engine under it — pace for the median, hold the ceiling as opportunism.' In two games out of three there is no kill, and in every game there is an engine: by turn 10 fodder arrives in 92.3% of games with a tutor, a free sac outlet in 92.1%, an ignition source in 90.6%, a drain in 85.4%, and the commander himself in 98.6% at a mean of turn 4.287. The engine is the median and the kill is the ceiling — but the ceiling is now reachable often enough that the pilot's job is to hold a tutor for it rather than to forget it exists. Turns 3 through 7 follow without ambiguity, and the instruction has changed shape: DO NOT HOLD PIECES WAITING TO ASSEMBLE. Turns 1-2: land, fast mana (85.8% by turn 10 with a tutor), and the cheapest renewable body — Bitterblossom on two is the single best play in the deck because it is the enabler class that gates everything. Turn 3: a fodder engine or an ignition source, never the drain, and never the tutor. Turn 4: Yawgmoth, which is when 72.1% of goldfish games cast him; hold Malakir Rebirth or Supernatural Stamina rather than casting a fourth body, because strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance prices the hub above the board. Turns 5-7: deploy the engine and draw off it, at INSTANT SPEED — Yawgmoth's ability needs no mana, so the correct habit is to activate on the last opponent's end step, which is strategy:tempo.sequencing's Commander correction made literal ('prefer committing at the end step before your own turn so the table's chances to respond are spent'). The tutor is spent LAST, once the board is stable and you know which half is missing, because strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors prices the alternative honestly — 'tutoring is fewer slots but costs board impact and a turn of tempo' — and a turn-three Demonic Tutor is a turn this deck cannot buy back. Deploy the drain last too, per strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window's 'sequence the scariest piece last so the deflection budget lasts until the turn you take it': a Yawgmoth plus a Bastion on the same board is the tell that redirects three players' removal onto you. And when the engine goes rather than the combo, go at ONE SEAT — seven drains per assembly against 40 life means the pod dies in sequence, twice verified (stacks 002 and 003), and strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window's 'Prefer win attempts that leave a rebuilt position if they fail' is satisfied every time, because a failed attempt leaves you holding the cards the attempt drew. One structural finding runs underneath all of it and deserves to be the issue's technical spine. Nest of Scarabs generates its value on token CREATION; Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat, Blood Artist and South Wind Avatar all meter DEATHS. Half of the hub's output is therefore unmonetised — the Insect has to die a second time to be worth anything, which is exactly why every engine stack ends by body exhaustion. Mirkwood Bats is the only card in the 99 whose trigger reads on creation ('Whenever you create or sacrifice a token, each opponent loses 1 life'), and Blasting Station is the only other card that notices a token entering at all, and only to untap. The rate that asymmetry pays is loop-specific and must not be flattened into one claim: Yawgmoth's cost is a SACRIFICE, so on that line Bats plausibly collects two triggers per activation; Blowfly Infestation's loop kills its tokens with -1/-1 counters and sacrifices nothing, so there Bats collects the creation half only, one trigger per iteration — half the rate, and still the difference between a drainless loop and a lethal one. Both readings are queued for the checker and neither is fact yet. Two tensions stay open and should be printed as tensions. South Wind Avatar is a Snake, and Ophiomancer makes a Snake only 'if you control no Snakes', so the deck's largest renewable fodder source and one of its four each-opponent drains switch each other off while both are on the battlefield; that conflict is smaller than it could be, and it is not solved. And the bracket floor of 4 rests half on four Game Changers, which is a fact, and half on eight two-card Mikaeus infinites, not one of which has ever been verified on this deck — a quarter of all games now route through that family with a tutor's help, while three Commander Spellbook claims about this exact list have already been overturned by the checker.
gaps: No aristocrats / sacrifice-loop section anywhere in the doc. Queries for 'sacrifice outlet aristocrats drain' top out at 0.247 against Budget, Proxies & Where Money Actually Binds — the doc has nothing on the outlet / fodder / payoff triad, which is this deck's entire architecture. This is the single largest hole a research pass could fill, and it generalises to every Aristocrats, Blood Artist and token-sacrifice deck in the format.

No theory of what BOUNDS an iterative engine. strategy:critical-mass.storm-math covers velocity and the go decision but not the question every stack on this deck answered: which resource runs out first — bodies, mana, life or library — and how to build so it is the one you can renew. All four engine stacks here ended by body exhaustion; the doc has no vocabulary for that finding.

Nothing on mana-free activated abilities. Yawgmoth's ability costs life and a body, not mana, which changes his behaviour under taxes, under Winter Orb, and at instant speed on opponents' end steps. strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial and strategy:tempo.sequencing both nearly reach this and neither names it.

No arithmetic for drain-as-clock in multiplayer. strategy:life-as-resource.philosophy-of-fire's Commander correction says reach 'must scale (each-opponent drains...)' but gives no numbers, so there is nothing to check '7 drains per assembly against 40 life' against. A section pricing each-opponent drains per assembly, and the 3.5x gap between 'each opponent' and 'target player' that stack 004 measured, would be immediately useful.

Token CREATION and creature DEATH as two distinct trigger economies, and the rate a creation payoff pays being loop-specific rather than a flat multiplier. The doc treats payoffs as one class. This deck shows they are not, that pairing a creation-heavy engine with death-only payoffs leaves half the engine unpaid, and that whether a loop SACRIFICES or merely kills changes the payoff rate by a factor of two.

No guidance on auditing ANTI-synergy. strategy:deckbuilding.cutting is about cutting duplicated function; nothing addresses two cards in a 99 that switch each other off, which is what South Wind Avatar does to Ophiomancer. A short section on conflict auditing would have flagged that before it was in the list.

No section on reading a simulated assembly rate — specifically on unassisted-versus-assisted pairs. strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors gives the hypergeometric arithmetic for copies and the k+1 heuristic for tutors, but nothing tells a reader that a 4.6% floor and a 31.4% tutor-assisted estimate are two different questions, that the gap between them is the tutor package's measured value, or that a tutor cannot fetch itself so the whole effect is capped by tutor-draw rate. strategy:combat-math.probability covers hypergeometrics and not interpretation.

Mono-colour deckbuilding as a constraint with a price. strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite demands breadth across five permanent classes; a mono-black deck can cover one and a half. The doc should say what the correct substitute is (sacrifice-based removal, deathtouch, a sideboard plan) rather than leaving the count looking like a build error.

Nothing on when an unverified combo should or should not set a deck's bracket. bracket_report forces floor 4 half on eight two-card infinites that no stack has confirmed, on a deck where the checker has already refuted three of the source's claims, and the tutor-assisted sim now routes a quarter of games through that same unverified family. strategy:deckbuilding.power-level.barometers covers what the rules say; it does not cover evidence quality.
